Manzur Morshed Khan and another-------Plaintiffs-Appellants
Vs
Bangladesh Bank and others--------Defendants –Respondents
full_judgment:
AKM Abdul Hakim J: In all these appeals the plaintiffs-appellants are different but the respondent nos. 1 and 2 and other respondents are different Banks and Financial Institutions, who sanctioned credit facilities to the respective plaintiff and plaintiffs of the suit filed present appeal before this court are common. The aforesaid appeals arose against the judgment and decree dated 10-7-2019 passed in Title Suit No. 298 of 2019, judgment and decree dated 20-5-2019 passed in Title Suit No. 284 of 2019, judgment and decree dated 20-2-2019 passed in Title Suit No. 103 of 2019, judgment and decree dated 5-5-2019 passed in Title Suit No. 248 of 2019, judgment and decree dated 24-7-2019 passed in Title Suit No. 380 of 2019, judgment and decree dated 24-7-2019 passed in Title Suit No. 381 of 2019, judgment and decree dated 20-2-2019 passed in Title Suit No. 111 of 2019, judgment and decree dated 20-2-2019 passed in Title Suit No. 112 of 2019, judgment and decree dated 5-5-2019 passed in Title Suit No. 250 of 2019, judgment and decree dated 7-7-2019 passed in Title Suit No. 317 of 2019, judgment and decree dated 18-2-2018 passed in Title Suit No. 91 of 2018 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka rejecting the respective plaints of the aforementioned suits under Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground of maintainability.

2. All these suits were filed for a declaration that the inclusion and publication of the names of the plaintiffs-appellants in the Credit Information Bureau (CIB) of Bangladesh Bank showing them as defaulters/guarantors in connection with the credit facilities is illegal, void, without legal effect and not binding upon the appellants-plaintiffs. But containing the similar facts and circumstances and involving the similar issues to the effect that after filing of the respective suits by the plaintiffs-appellants before the Joint District Judge without issuing any summons or notice fixed the suit for maintainability and hearing of injunction application which were filed by the respective parties before the court below. In view of such position all these appeals were heard together and dispose of by a single judgment.

3. The plaint case of aforesaid suits filed by the respective plaintiff are more or less same. The defendant No. 1, Bangladesh Bank and defendant No. 2, General Manager CIB of Bangladesh Bank is responsible for publishing CIB Report naming the loan defaulters and other defendants are the bank and financial Institutions are different in all the suits. Basically, the case stated in the plaint by different plaintiffs are similar. In the plaint, it is stated that the provisions of publishing the names of the defaulters in the CIB Report of Bangladesh Bank as provided under Article 42-48 of the Bangladesh Bank order, 1972 and Section 27 Ka Ka of the Bank Companies Act, 1991 are absolutely unconstitutional, ultra vires and violative of the fundamental rights as guaranteed under Article 31, 32, 40 and 42 of the constitution of the people's Republic of Bangladesh. It is further stated that in case of defaulting issue, the Bank or financial Institution has several legal recourses including filing suits under Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and filing other Civil and Criminal Cases. In the plaints it is also stated that due to non-payment of loan, the respective Bank and financial institutions sent the name of the plaintiff or plaintiffs to the defendant No. 1 as classified as Bad/loss and defendant No. 2 published the name of the plaintiff as "Defaulter" in CIB list. Due to arbitrariness in sending the name of the plaintiffs in the CIB list, business grow a deal lock position and has been suffering hugs loss. As such the plaintiffs prayed for a declaration that the impugned classification and publication of the name of the respective plaintiff in the CIB report of Bangladesh Bank is arbitrary, illegal, void, without legal effect and not binding upon the plaintiffs.

4. At the time of filing of the suit the plaintiffs also filed an application for temporary injunction. The learned Joint District Judge fixed next date for hearing on maintainability of the suit and injunction hearing.

5. Ultimately, the learned Joint District Judge passed the impugned judgment and order rejected the plaint under Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground of maintainability mainly relying upon three decisions reported in 18 DLR 709, 48 DLR (AD) 50 and 51 DLR (AD) 221.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Dhaka in the respective suit as clearly described in the Memorandum of the respective appeal. The order rejecting the plaint is a decree within the meaning of section 2(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure the plaintiffs of the respective suits preferred the aforesaid appeals against the judgment and decree more fully described in the respective Memorandum of Appeal.

7. At the time of filing of the present appeal, the appellant of all the appeal also filed an application under Order XXXIX, rule 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure for an order of temporary injunction restraining the defendants-respondents from reporting, sending and publishing the names of the plaintiffs-appellants in the CIB report of the Bangladesh Bank showing them as defaulters in connection of the credit facilities advanced by the defendants-respondents. Upon hearing, this court issued separate rule upon the opposite-parties to show cause and restrained the respondents-opposite parties by an order of ad-interim injunction as stated above.

8. In view of the averments made in the plaint and the reliefs sought for, now the pertinent question which call for determination in these appeal is to see whether the learned Joint District Judge committed any illegality in rejecting the plaint on the ground of maintainability under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure while the suit was also fixed for hearing temporary injunction.

9. Ms Syeda Nasrin, learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiffs-appellants in First Appeal No. 424 of 2019, First Appeal No. 450 of 2019 and First Appeal No. 461 of 2019 submits that the trial court erroneously rejected the plaint and dismissed the suit on the question of maintainability by invoking the jurisdiction under Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure. She further submits that the question of maintainability of the suit could be decided only after framing issues under Order XIV, rule 2 and Order XV, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure and that the maintainability of the suit can be determined at the time of trial and not under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. She next submits that the learned Joint District Judge totally misappreciated and misconstrued the provisions of Article 41(1) of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972 erroneously rejected the plaint on this ground of maintainability. She also submits that the trial court committed a gross error of law in rejecting the plaint suo-moto and dismissed the suit without any application filed by the defendants under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. She finally submits that maintainability of a suit being a mixed question of fact, the same cannot be decided before filing of the written statement by the defendants. In support her submissions learned Advocate relied on the decisions reported in 30 DLR (SC) 30, 48 DLR 367 and 11 MLR (AD) 2006 58.

10. In First Appeal No. 424 of 2019, Mr Shahjada Al-Amin Kabir, learned Advocate for the respondent No. 8, Mr SM Kamal Hossain Moni, learned Advocate for the respondent No. 9 and Mr KS Salah Uddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the respondent No. 15 filed power on 29-1-2020 and 6-2-2020 respectively but none of them was present before the court at the time of hearing of the Appeal.

11. Mr AKM Fakrul Islam with learned Advocate Mr Redwan Ahmed appeared for the plaintiffs-appellants in First Appeal No. 422 of 2019 and First Appeal No. 308 of 2019 has submitted that the learned Joint District Judge by the impugned judgment and order rejected the plaint on the ground of maintainability which is not specifically provided under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the ingredience upon which a plaint can be rejected on the said rule is no way applicable in the present case. He further submitted that the civil court has wide jurisdiction to examine whether the Bangladesh Bank rightly declared the plaintiff as loan defaulter and published his name in CIB report and that matter should be decided by the civil court. Learned Advocate in support of his submission has relied on the decision reported in I BLC (AD) 159. He also submitted that the trial court wrongly decided the question of maintain-ability without framing proper issues. He finally submitted that there is no express provision in section 27KaKa of the Banking Companies Act. 1991, that the defaulter cannot invoke jurisdiction in civil court declaring that he is defaulter or not. He further contended that Article 41(1) of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972 has no manner application in respect of sending the names of the plaintiff to publish in the CM report under section 27KaKa of the Bank Companies Act, 1991.

12. In First Appeal No. 425 of 2019 Mr Md Nurul Amin, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellant has submitted that the learned Advocate Ms Syeda Nasrin has touched and raised all the points regarding provisions of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and cited several decisions of our apex court. He contends further that the learned Joint District Judge committed gross error of law in rejecting the plaint without applying its judicial mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and the decisions of our Apex Court.

13. In First Appeal No. 422 of 2019, Mr Elen Emon Shah, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-respondent No. 3. He find very difficult to oppose the submissions advanced by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellant. He tried to submit that the plaint of the suit is clearly barred by law under section 41(1) of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972. He further submits that declaration from a court is not at all necessary for sending the name of defaulting borrower to Bangladesh Bank under section 27KaKa of the Bank Company Act, 1991. Mr Elen Emon Shah, in support of his arguments has relied the case of Al-Amin Bread and Biscuits Ltd. vs Bangladesh Bank, reported in 17 BLC 653.

14. The learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-appellant in First Appeal No. 314 of 2019, 131-132 of 2019 and 98 of 2018 adopted the submissions of Ms Syeda Nasrin and the decisions referred to above by Ms Syeda Nasrin in support of her contention as the points in issue are similar.

15. It appears that in First Appeal No. 450 of 2019, 461 of 2019, 132 of 2019, 425 of 2019 no one appears for the respondents although notice was duly served upon them.

16. Learned Advocate Md Abul Kalam Azad appeared for respondent No. 4 in First Appeal No. 314 of 2019, Mr Shahjada Al-Amin, learned Advocate appeared for respondent No. 8, in First Appeal No. 308 of 2019, Mr Tushar Kanti Das, Advocate, Mr Monjur Kader, Advocate, Mr KS Salah-uddin Ahmed, Advocate, Mr lftekhar Ahmed, Advocate appeared for the respondent nos. 3/4/5/6 respectively, Mr Shaikh Mohammad Zakir Hossain, Advocate and Shahjada Al-Amin, Advocate filed power on behalf of respondent No. 3 and respondent No. 4 respectively. But none of the Advocate for respondents were present before the court at the time of hearing of the Appeal.

17. It appears that in all the suits after registration of the suit no summons was issued upon the defendants and in some suits impugned judgment and order was passed by the learned Joint District Judge by referring/relying 3 (three) decisions reported in 18 DLR 709, 48 DLR (AD) 50 and 51 DLR (AD) 221, which are in fact different from the facts, circumstances, related laws and other issues of the present case. The differences are summarized below:

18. In BSRS vs Rahman Textile Mills, 51 DLR (AD) 221 (shortly referred as `BSRS Case')- By the majority decision the plaint was rejected upon an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure filed by the defendants. But in the present suits, the plaint was rejected just after registration of the suit and before issuing summon/notice upon the defendants.

19. In BSRS case, the plaint was rejected not for the contents of the plaint or barred by any law but on the ground that the very reliefs claimed in the suit are specifically barred under Article 34(5)(a)(i) or (ii) or (iii) of Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha Order, 1972 (Presidents Order No. 128 of 1972). The reliefs were barred under law, thus plaint was barred by law for seeking barred reliefs under law. But in the present cases, the reliefs claimed by the plaintiffs are not barred under any law.

20. In BSRS case, it was further observed that article 34 of President's Order No.128 of 1972 is an independent, substantive and procedural provision regarding bar of entertainment of a suit on grounds different from those described in Order VII, rule 11 Code of Civil Procedure. Article 34(5) specifically lays down that if the prayers in the suit are of the description contained in Article 34(5)(a)(i) or (ii) or (iii) then the suit will not be entertained. In an ordinary civil suit the plaint is rejected, inter alia, "where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law." Therefore in an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure the statement in the plaint has to be looked into to determine if the suit if barred by any law. But under Article 34(5) it is not the statement in the plaint but the reliefs claimed in the suit under Article 34(5)(a)(i) or (ii) or (iii) which will determine whether the suit is entertainable or not. Under Order VII, rule 11 Code of Civil Procedure it is the statement in the plaint which is the determining factor but under Article 34(5) it is the relief claimed which is the determining factor.

21. In the said case, it was also observed that the instant cases are governed by Article 34(5) of Presidents Order No.128 of 1972. To the extent that the determining factors of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and Article 34(5) are different and inconsistent, the provisions of Article 34(5) will prevail over those of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The defendant-appellant need not have filed application under Order VII, rule 11 Code of Civil Procedure. It could have maintained application under Article 34(5) of President's Order No. 128 of 1972.

22. The stages of BSRS case and the present suit are completely different. The former one was long after filing of the suit, service of summons, after appearing of the parties and contesting the same but in the present cases it was only on the preliminary stage after registration of the suit, where no summons/notice were served, defendants did not appear, and none contested the suit.

23. In WB Industrial Corp vs Deen Mohammad, 48 DLR (AD) 50 (shortly referred to as 'WB Case)—The plaint was rejected by the trial court because there was an application filed by the defendant under Order VII, rule 11 before the Court below on the ground that the suit is barred under Article 34(5) of the Bangladesh Shilpa Bank Order, 1972 (President's Order No. 129 of 1972). But in the present suits, the plaint was rejected suo moto.

24. In this case, though the plea of malafide was taken, however the Court did not allow the plea of malafide and bonafide saying that the issue of malafide or bonafide involved disputed question of fact which required continuation of the suit, and the plaint was rejected on different ground arising out of the ouster provision of law. That ouster provision barred the parties from claiming certain reliefs. But in the present cases, the plaint was rejected suo moto without having any such ouster clause under law. The reliefs prayed in the present suit are not barred under any law.

25. The stage of WB case and the present suit are completely different. The former one was long after filing this suit, service of summons, appearing by the parties and contesting the same; but in the latter case it was only on the preliminary stage just after registration of the suit without issuance of any summon upon the defendants.

26. In the case of Burmah Eastern Ltd vs Burmah Eastern Employees Union, 18 DLR 709 (shortly referred to as 'Burmah Eastern Case )— In that case the plaint was rejected upon the application filed by the defendant Burmah Eastern Ltd. under Order VII, rule 11. But in the present suits, the plaint was rejected suo moto.

27. In Burmah Eastern case, the plaintiff have no 'legal character' or 'status', in filing the suit very question of 'legal character' was questioned. But in the present suits plaintiff have legal character or status, no such question was raised as to 'legal character' of the parties as well as 'nature of the suit'.

28. In the said case, the Court came to the conclusion that from the mere perusal of the plaint, it appeared prohibited as well as barred under and by law. But in the present suits there is no such specific prohibition under law in filing the present suit.

29. The stages of Burmah Eastern and the present suit are completely different. The former one was long after filing the suit, service of summons, appearing by the parties and contesting the same; but in the present cases it was only on the preliminary stage after registered in a register of Civil Suits under Order IV, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure without issuing any summons upon the defendants.

30. Therefore, it appears that the learned trial court below was out of total misreading, misconception and misconstrued the aforesaid cases erroneously applied the ratio in the present case very arbitrarily and also without applying judicial mind.

31. Although the learned Joint District Judge rejected the plaint on the ground of maintain-ability but the above noted decisions as referred by the learned Joint District Judge have no nexus in the facts and circumstances of the present case.

32. On the other hand, the learned Joint District Judge failed to take notice of the following latest decisions relating to the rejection of plaint by our Apex Court reported in 11 MLR (AD) (2006) 58, 4 MLR (AD) (1999) 426 and 30 DLR (SC) 30.

1) 11 MLR (AD) (2006) 58, Wherein it has been held: "Rejection of plaint on ground of maintainability of the Suit is not permissible before filing of written statement

"Preliminary issue as to the maintain-ability of the suit cannot be decided before filing of written statement."

2) 4 MLR (AD) (1999) 426: "Maintain-ability of the suit can be determined at the time of trial and not under Order VII, rule II of the Code of Civil Procedure. Plaint cannot be rejected in limine under Order VII, rule 11 CPC on the question of maintainability of the suit."

3) 30 DLR (SC) 30: The Supreme Court has observed that if a court finds that a suit may be decided on the decision of an issue of law only, the court may try that issue first and may dispose of the suit. The court also observed that rule 2 of order XIV was an exception to general rule prohibiting disposed of a suit piecemeal.

The court further observed that special provision made in Order 14, rule 2 and Order 15, rule 3 form exceptions to the general rule prohibiting disposal of a suit piecemeal.

The main consideration underlying the general rule which deprecates piecemeal trial is to avoid a protracted litigation and unnecessary expenditure. The reason behind the special provisions of the Code which seek to give priority to the determination of certain issues before taking up the hearing of other issues appears to be also precisely the same namely, economy of time and expenses. These special provisions are contained in Order 14, rule 2 and Order 15, rule 3 of the Code and there is hardly any doubt that the main object behind these provisions is the shortening of time and the lessening of expenditure.

As we have already noticed, the provision of Order 14, rule 2 is clearly obligatory but under Order 15, rule 3 of the Code the Court has kind of discretion.

33. In the impugned judgments the learned Joint District Judge found that the suit is explicitly barred by Article 41(1) of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972. To appreciate this findings, it will be profitable to quote the Article 41(1) of the Bangladesh Bank Order 1972 which provides that—

"41.—(1) No suit or other legal proceedings shall lie against the Bank or any of its Officer for anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done in pursuance of Article 36 or Article 37 or Article 38 or Article 39 or Article 40 or in pursuance of the provisions of Chapter IV.

(2) No suit or other legal proceedings shall lie against the Bank or any of its Officers for any damage caused or likely to be caused by anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done in pursuance of Article 36 or Article 37 or Article 38 or Article 39 or Article 40, or in pursuance of the provisions of Chapter IV."

34. The very words 'good faith' are the riders of Article 41 which are ultimately providing some sort of indemnity or liberty or exemption to the bank or its officers from any suit or legal proceeding for any kind of work or performance in pursuance of some provisions of law thereof done/carried out in course of duty. In no way, it restricts/prohibits/precludes/bars upon filing any suit or other legal proceedings in case of 'dispute' arising between the borrower and the creditor bank. Article 41 does not create any express or implied bar upon any relief or contents of a pleading. Thus reliefs prayed in the present suit are in no way barred under Article 41.

35. Definition of good faith is not given in the Bangladesh Bank Order. "Good Faith" as denified in section 3(20) of the General Clauses Act, 1897. "Section 3(20) Speaks: a thing shall be deemed to be done in "good faith" where it is in fact done honestly, whether it is done negligently or not." But it transpires that dispute in the suit does not come within the definition of good faith. It is a 'dispute' of civil nature which is to be adjudicated by adducing proper evidence and witnesses before the Court of law. But the learned trial court failed to appreciate this difference, and erroneously rejected the plaint on misconception of law by referring Article 41 of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972.

36. In this connection, we have carefully examined the decision reported in 17 BLC 653 as cited by the learned Advocate Mr Elen Emon Shah but the facts and circumstances of the above decision and instant case are completely distinguishable and, as such, this decision has no manner of application in the present case. Therefore, decision does not have any nexus because of the fact that same was passed in writ petition not in a civil suit. Moreover, this decision does not create any bar upon filing a civil suit by any person whose name is published in the CIB report.

37. At this juncture, it can be said that Article 41 does not create any bar upon any relief, and it has no application under Order VII, rule 11(d). The learned courts below totally failed to appreciate such important aspect of the case.

38. Order VII, rule 11 describes the procedure for rejection of plaint. It is necessary to quote Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure which reads as under:—

"11. The plaint shall be rejected in the following cases:—

(a) where it does not disclose a cause of action;

(b) where the relief claimed is undervalued, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the Court fails to do so;

(c) where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so;

(d) where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law.

[Provided that the time fixed by the Court for the correction of the valuation or supplying of the requisite stamp-paper shall not exceed twenty-one days]

[(e) where any of the provisions of rule 9(1A) is not complied with and the plaintiff on being required by the Court to comply therewith within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so.]"

39. On a close reading of the aforesaid rule, it is evident that under five circumstances, a plaint shall be rejected:

a. where it does not disclose any cause of action;.

b. where the relief claimed is undervalued and the plaintiff fails to correct the valuation within the time fixed by the court:

c. where the plaint is insufficiently stamped and the plaintiff fails to put in requisite stamp papers within the time fixed by the court;

d. where from the statement in the plaint the suit appears to be barred by any law;

e. where any provisions of rule 9 (1A) is not complied with within the time fixed by the court.

40. It has been held in the case of Bangladesh Jatiya Samabaya Shilpa Samity Ltd. vs Shan Hosiety, Proprietor Md Abu Taleb, reported in 2004 (12) BLT (AD) 253 = 10 BLC (AD) 8, which is quoted below—

"With regard to rejection of plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the High Court Division rightly found that in deciding the question as to whether a plaint is liable to be rejected the court is always required to peruse the plaint only and court is not permitted to travel beyond the plaint to dig out grounds to reject the plaint which is a settled principle of law."

41. While disposing of a case concerning rejection of plaint, Justice Fazle Munim, Chief Justice in paragraph No. 46 observed that—If the court does not even persue the plaint and rejects outright the door of arbitrariness is opened and whatever little right a citizen left with is reduced to shadow substances. Reference: 39 DLR (AD) 1.

42. Further, after scrutinizing the series of decisions of our Apex Court in respect of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, we may refer some of decisions reported in 39 DLR (AD) 1, 42 DLR (AD) 244, 49 DLR 531, 564, 53 DLR (AD) 62, 54 DLR (AD) 125 and 57 DLR (AD) 18 wherein the principles laid down as under:

(i) The well settled principle of laws relating to Order VII, rule 11 are the plaint can be rejected only on reference to plaint itself as whether it is barred in any of the four clauses of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

(ii) Plaint cannot be rejected on defense material as well as on mixed question of law and fact.

(iii) Where evidence is required and where there is material, plaint cannot be rejected.

(iv)Plaint can be rejected if it does not disclose a cause of action and barred by any law.

(v) There is no hard and fast Rule when an application for rejection of plaint is to be filed but ends of justice demands that it must be filed at the earliest opportunity.

(vi) Plaint cannot be rejected before filing of the written statement.

43. Now, let us consider whether the court can reject a plaint under section 151 under inherent power of the court even the provisions of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure are found not to be applicable.

44. In the case of Abdul Jalil vs Islamic Bank Bangladesh Limited, reported in 53 DLR (AD) 12, it has been held that:—

"Now it is a well settled principle of law that if the continuation of the suit is found to be an abuse of the process of the court, if the suit is foredoomed or if the ultimate result of the suit is as clear as the day light, the suit should be buried at its inception by rejecting the plaint by invoking inherent powers of the Court provided under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure."

45. Further, on perusal of the facts of the present case, it appears to be distinguishable from the case reported in 53 DLR (AD) 12. In exceptional situation a plaint can be rejected under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure even if it does not come within the mischief of the Rule, but such situation is totally absent in the present case.

46. Before rejecting a plaint under Order VII, rule 11, it is desirable to give an opportunity to the plaintiff to remove the defect in the plaint. In a case reported in 58 DLR (AD) 219, the Appellate Division has observed that instead of straightway rejecting a plaint, the plaintiff should be allowed to remove any formal defect therein and suitably amend the plaint to make it maintainable and to get the relief in a single suit.

<u>47. A suit for declaration is maintainable under section 42 as, to any legal character or to any right as to any property of the plaintiff if the defendant denies or is interested to deny his or her title to such character or right. If the above conditions are satisfied, the plaintiff does not need to ask for any further relief than a mere declaration.</u>

<u>48. The concept of 'legal character' in section 42 is wide enough to include the status of a person. In order to entitle the plaintiff to bring a suit under section 42, 'it is riot necessary that the defendant should actually deny the plaintiff's legal, character. If the claim which might be sent up by the defendant is a hindrance to the plaintiff in the exercise of his or her rights or would expose him or her to liability if he or she disregarded, he or she might come to Court for a declaration that the claim so set up by the defendant was not well founded. Thus, 'legal character' denotes a personal and special right not arising out of contract or tort, but of legal recognition. For example, rejection of plaintiff's application for allotment may create legal recognition enforce-able against a person whose similar application is accepted.</u>

49. We have examined the plaint and considered the submissions advanced by the learned Advocate of respective parties, relevant provision of the Code of Civil Procedure, Bangladesh Bank Orders, 1972, Bank Companies Act, 1991 and decisions of our Apex Court very carefully.

50. It appears from the order sheet of the respective suits that after registration of the respective suits, and next date was fixed for maintainability of the suit and hearing temporary injunction matter. Ultimately, the learned Joint District Judge passed an order rejecting the plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground of maintainability. In the order, the learned Joint District Judge erroneously found that the suit is barred by law under section 41(1) of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972.

<u>51. We have already held earlier part of the judgment that the learned Joint District Judge acted most illegally in rejecting the plaint on the ground of maintainability on the assumption of facts which are not borne out by the plaint and also sanctioned by law. That the civil court has wide jurisdiction to examine whether the Bangladesh Bank rightly declared the appellants as loan defaulter and published their names in the CIB report and that matter should be decided by the trial court after framing issue on it.</u>

52. In the back ground of the discussions, relevant provisions of law involved in this suit and the decisions cited above, we are of the view that the learned Joint District Judge wrongly decided the question of maintainability and rejected the plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. We therefore, find that the aforesaid judgment and decree passed by the Fifth Joint District Judge, Dhaka cannot be sustained and same is liable to be set-aside.

53. In the result, all the appeals are allowed without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree dated 10-7-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 298 of 2019, the judgment and decree dated 20-5-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 284 of 2019, the judgment and decree dated 20-2-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 103 of 2019, the judgment and decree dated 5-5-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 248 of 2019, the judgment and decree dated 24-7-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 380 of 2019, the judgment and decree dated 24-7-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 381 of 2019, the judgment and decree dated 20-2-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 111 of 2019, the judgment and decree dated 20-2-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 112 of 2019, the judgment and decree dated 05-5-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 250 of 2019, the judgment and decree dated 07-7-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 317 of 2019 and the judgment and decree dated 18-2-2018 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 91 of 2018 all are hereby set-aside and the connected Rules being Nos. Civil Rule 514(F) of 2019, Civil Rule 548(F) of 2019, Civil Rule 338(F) of 2019, Civil Rule 343(F) of 2019, Civil Rule 547(F) of 2019, Civil Rule 546(F) of 2019, Civil Rule 144(F) of 2019, Civil Rule 143(F) of 2019, Civil Rule 342(F) of 2019, Civil Rule 550(F) of 2019, are made absolute without any order as to cost.

54. Considering the facts and circumstance of the case the trial court is directed to proceed with the respective suits filed the plaintiffs-appellants in accordance with law.
